newsitem.title: UK: Latest Blenheim bid talk has little impact.
newsitem.headline: Latest Blenheim bid talk has little impact.

text.p: Speculation that Reed-Elsevier might launch a 530p a share bid for Blenheim Group Plc fell largely on deaf ears on Thursday in a market fast becoming hardened to rumours surrounding the Blenheim group.

A report in the Daily Mail on Thursday that Reed has offered 530p a share for the exhibitions organiser failed to significantly lift shares, reflecting unease at the inceasing number of stories surrounding Blenheim, said analysts.
However, they noted that if today's story did prove to be true, then an offer of 530p a share would almost certainly be approved by the Blenheim board.
"If Reed did put a 530p a share bid on the table, I think it would get approval from the Blenheim board," said Anthony de Larrinaga, a media analyst at Panmure Gordon.
A Reed company spokesman declined comment on the latest bout of speculation, while industry sources commented that "there was nothing in the story."
"It is very difficult to know what is and isn't a genuine story anymore," said one sector analyst who requested anonymity.
"It strikes me as slightly bizarre that a couple of days after someone has paid 500p and got a stake very easily that someone else would need to go and pay 530," he added.

The analyst was referring to VNU, a Dutch publishing group, that took a 15 percent stake in Blenheim on Tuesday at 500 pence per share, well above the 480p Reed-Elsevier was rumoured to have been talking about with Blenheim prior to the VNU acquisition.
VNU called the move a strategic long term investment and said it had no current intention of making an offer for Blenheim, barring rival offers for the firm.
Analysts said that if a 530p a share bid were to emerge from Reed, the level of acceptances the company asked for would be the crucial factor in securing the deal.
"The problem is that VNU remains a wild card. It would be a question of who can bluff who. VNU would obviously like to take over Blenheim ultimately," said de Larrinaga.

Analysts said if Reed made a bid that was conditional on acceptances of 90 percent then VNU would obviously have the potential to scupper the bid, while a request for 50 percent acceptances is seen more likely to prompt VNU to dispose of its stake and take profit.
At 30p a share profit that would give VNU a return of around four million stg before expenses, analysts estimate.

Under takeover rules, if VNU were to make a formal bid it would have to be pitched at or above the price it paid for any stake of 10 percent and above and would be have to seven days after the original stake purchase.
By 1119 GMT, Blenheim shares were quoted 6p higher at 463-1/2, but were off earlier highs.
